title: Madhya Pradesh Cabinet Approves Uniform Civil Code Bill as Assembly Session Opens Today
excerpt: The bill, modelled on Uttarakhand's UCC, bans polygamy across religions and mandates registration of live-in relationships, with penalties of up to five years in prison.
body:
• Madhya Pradesh's cabinet unanimously approved the UCC Bill-2026 on Sunday, clearing it for introduction in the Assembly session beginning July 20.
  • The bill bans polygamy for all religions and imposes up to five years' imprisonment for married individuals in live-in relationships.
  • Scheduled Tribes are fully exempt from the law, and succession provisions have been simplified from roughly 100 clauses to 30.
  • If passed during the five-day session ending July 25, MP will become India's second state after Uttarakhand to implement a Uniform Civil Code.

Cabinet Clears Draft in Symbolic Jagdishpur Meeting

The Madhya Pradesh government moved decisively on Sunday when Chief Minister Mohan Yadav convened a cabinet meeting at Jagdishpur — the historic town he renamed from Islamnagar earlier this year — to secure unanimous approval for the draft Uniform Civil Code Bill-2026.

"The cabinet has wholeheartedly and unanimously approved the UCC Bill-2026," Yadav told reporters after the meeting. He framed the legislation as rooted in Indian constitutional values, citing Article 44, which places a Uniform Civil Code among the Directive Principles of State Policy.

The bill will be tabled on the floor of the Assembly during the monsoon session, which runs from July 20 to July 24. If the BJP-controlled legislature passes it during this window, Madhya Pradesh will become the second Indian state to implement a UCC, following Uttarakhand's landmark enactment in 2024.

What the Bill Contains

The draft legislation is modelled closely on Uttarakhand's UCC framework. Retired Supreme Court Justice Ranjana Prakash Desai, who chaired Uttarakhand's drafting committee, also heads Madhya Pradesh's six-member panel, which was constituted in April 2026 and submitted its report after consulting communities across the state.

Key provisions include the abolition of polygamy across all religions. Under existing law, the Hindu Marriage Act already prohibits polygamy for Hindus, while Muslim Personal Law permits men to marry up to four women under certain conditions. The UCC would impose a uniform rule: no person may marry again while a spouse is alive unless legally divorced.

"If Ram marries once, why should Rahim marry two or four times? Only those who marry once will be able to live in Madhya Pradesh."

— Mohan Yadav, Chief Minister of Madhya Pradesh

The bill also mandates registration of live-in relationships, mirroring Uttarakhand's approach. Married individuals entering live-in relationships without disclosure face penalties of up to five years in prison. The drafting committee streamlined succession-related provisions from approximately 100 clauses to 30, making the legislation more accessible to the public.

Scheduled Tribes remain completely exempt from the bill's provisions, preserving tribal customary law — a significant political and legal carve-out that Uttarakhand also adopted.

Opposition Gears Up for Floor Fight

The monsoon session is expected to be contentious. The Congress-led opposition has signalled plans to raise multiple issues, including the Ujjain land purchase controversy, farmer compensation for Ken-Betwa project displacement, and the NEET-UG paper leak scandal.

Leader of Opposition Umang Singhar will seek a discussion on fertiliser shortages ahead of the kharif sowing season. The UCC bill itself is likely to face sustained debate, with the opposition questioning its timing and constitutional implications.

What This Means for NRIs

For Indians abroad, the UCC debate touches on fundamental questions about personal law — marriage, divorce, inheritance, and succession — that affect diaspora families navigating legal systems across multiple countries. A state-level UCC simplifies legal frameworks for NRIs with property, family ties, or planned returns to Madhya Pradesh, though its interaction with central personal laws and other state jurisdictions remains an open question.

The BJP has long championed a nationwide UCC as part of its core legislative agenda. With Uttarakhand already implementing one and Gujarat's draft reportedly in progress, the Madhya Pradesh bill represents another step in what the party frames as the "One Nation, One Law" vision — a trajectory that NRI communities, particularly those with cross-state family and property interests, are watching closely.
